title: What to prepare for customer-service AI approval
summary: Prepare the data flows, access scope, findings, procurement path and named sign-offs your team needs to assess a customer-service AI deployment.
body_markdown:
Published October 3, 2026 · Updated October 16, 2026


A promising customer-service AI pilot gives a business a reason to consider a wider investment. Moving into production is a larger commitment: funding a continuing service, choosing a supplier and entrusting live customer work to the agreed setup. A pilot's results can inform those decisions, but cannot settle all of them.


Each decision needs its own owner. The business sponsor and budget owner assess the investment; procurement manages the buying process; the service owner needs evidence to authorize go-live, with the required technical, security and privacy reviews. The same person may hold more than one role, but approving the spend and authorizing live operation remain separate decisions. Confirm who holds each in your organization.


An approval pack should connect the proposed service and its evidence to those decisions, so a promising pilot has a clear route to production and unresolved questions remain visible. The structure below is our recommendation, informed by Typewise assessment and implementation conversations in 2026. It is not a legal compliance checklist or a guarantee of approval.


## Show the actual data flow


Draw the route from the customer's request through each system to the response. For every step, record what data moves, where it is processed, what is stored and for how long.


During an assessment with one of our enterprise customers, the security reviewer asked whether personal data reached Typewise before anonymization. The important distinction was where that step happened, not merely whether anonymization appeared on a feature list. The question itself did not establish that the design was approved.


Show the proposed design as it is. If identifiers are removed upstream, explain how the workflow will still find the correct order or produce the required reply. Mark an unresolved design choice as unresolved rather than drawing it as an implemented control.


Separate infrastructure evidence from application evidence. Ask what a certificate or report actually covers, then provide the relevant information about application access, identity, logging and retention. Use current documentation rather than a remembered answer from a demo.


## State the scope in actions people can assess


"Integrates with the shop" is too vague. "Reads order status for the authenticated customer's own orders" gives an assessor something to examine.


List the data the AI may read and the actions it may perform for each workflow. Mark whether a person reviews every output or whether the AI can act autonomously. Include what is excluded and what happens when the system cannot complete a request.


In the enterprise assessment, the coordinator asked whether one assessment could cover both the reviewed assistant and a second, not-yet-live use case. Do not assume approval for one mode covers another. Ask the responsible team which changes require reassessment and record its answer.


The[permissions guide](https://www.typewise.app/blog/customer-service-ai-agent-permissions) covers how those agreed boundaries must be enforced during operation.


## Give each finding an owner and a decision


Keep the vendor's answers, model and hosting details, subprocessors and supporting documents together, with their dates. A call can clarify an answer, but the person completing an assessment needs a record they can use afterward.


For each finding, record the affected scope, evidence, responsible owner and next decision. Depending on your process, that may mean fixing it before launch, removing the affected workflow, deferring or rejecting the deployment, or asking the authorized risk owner to consider a residual risk.


A risk owner cannot waive a mandatory requirement simply by recording acceptance. Likewise, a remediation plan is not permission to launch. Keep the final go-live sign-off separate and obtain it through your organization's process.


## Agree the procurement path beyond the pilot


One of our retail customers reported that its proposed pilot had been stopped for formal procurement because of the spend anticipated afterward. The procurement scope had also grown beyond the initial experiment. The account describes a process constraint, not a rejection of AI's usefulness.


Before investing in a pilot, ask what continuing it would require. Does the expected scope need a tender, a new contract, an integration review or a separate budget decision? Identify the people who decide and the evidence they will need.


Do not assume the pilot sponsor has authority over the eventual purchase or the technology stack. Record both the business decision and the technical decision.


## End with a bounded launch decision


Summarize the pilot stages, the work allowed in each stage, the evidence needed to advance and the conditions that stop it. Include results for correct completion, partial and full handoffs, and severe errors in the cases tested, with the sample size, request types and unresolved findings. Those results support a decision about the tested scope, not every future request. Name the people responsible for support, monitoring and incident response. Link the full[go-live plan](https://www.typewise.app/blog/how-support-teams-go-live-with-ai) rather than repeating it in every questionnaire.


Before the approval meeting, ask each decision-maker to check the pack for missing evidence. Leave open questions visible. The useful outcome is an explicit decision about this scope, including any conditions, rather than a general statement that the organization is "comfortable with AI."
